readerTitle: How Superhuman turned a fuzzy feeling into a number
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Superhuman, 창업자 Rahul Vohra의 공개 글) + 가상 적용 (소상공인 대상 기장 대행 회사)
insight: 제품-시장 적합성은 감으로 아는 것이 아니라, '이 제품이 없어지면 얼마나 아쉬울까'를 고객군별로 재서 무엇을 만들지 정하는 데 쓰는 숫자다.
misconception: 적합성은 오면 저절로 느껴진다. 점수가 낮으면 모든 고객의 요청을 골고루 들어줘서 평균 만족도를 올려야 한다.

sources.text: Vohra, R. (2018). How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit. First Round Review. (22% 시작 점수, 고객군 나누기, 로드맵 절반 배분, 58% 도달의 출처)
Sean Ellis의 '매우 실망' 설문과 40% 기준. Ellis, S. & Brown, M. (2017). Hacking Growth. 및 Sean Ellis의 공개 글
가상 적용 사례 (기장 대행 회사)의 모든 수치는 설명용

factChecks.note: 시작 점수 22%와 이후 58% 도달은 Vohra(2018) First Round Review 글 기준입니다. 게시 전에 원문 수치와 기간(약 1년 미만)을 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 기간을 구체적으로 적지 않았습니다.
고객군을 좁혔을 때의 중간 점수는 원문에서 약 33%(32~33%)로 기억되지만 정확한 소수점은 확인이 필요합니다. 카드에는 "about a third"로만 적었습니다.
'매우 실망' 응답이 몰린 고객군(창업자, 경영진, 관리자, 사업개발 담당자)과 핵심 이점이 '속도'였다는 내용은 원문 기준입니다. 원문 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
로드맵의 절반은 열성 고객이 좋아하는 점 강화, 절반은 '약간 실망' 고객의 걸림돌 해결에 썼다는 배분은 원문 기준입니다. 설문을 시작한 시점(2017년경)은 카드에 적지 않았습니다.
40% 기준은 Sean Ellis가 여러 스타트업의 설문 결과를 비교해 얻은 경험칙입니다. 비교한 회사 수 등 세부 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
가상 사례 계산: 전체 25%, 식당 고객군 50%. 모두 설명용 가상 수치이며 계산식은 필요 없습니다.

cards.title: How Superhuman turned a fuzzy feeling into a number
body: Most founders answer "Do we have product-market fit?" with a gut feeling.
Rahul Vohra, founder of the premium email app Superhuman, wanted something better. Before a wide launch, he looked for a way to measure fit, track it, and steer by it.

image.label: A founder holding a gauge with a needle near the middle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노트북 앞의 창업자가 커다란 계기판을 들여다보고, 바늘은 왼쪽(낮은 값)과 가운데 사이에 있음. 화면에는 이메일 목록만 흐릿하게. 실제 Superhuman 로고나 UI는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Only 22% would be very disappointed.
body: You run an invite-only email app. You ask early users: *How would you feel if you could no longer use it?* Only 22% answer "very disappointed." A common rule of thumb says fit starts around 40%.
What do you do next?

options.text: Collect requests from every unhappy user and build the most popular ones
options.feedback: You'll learn a lot, but you may spend months pleasing people who will never love the product, while the fans wait.

options.text: Study who said "very disappointed," then build for them and for people like them
options.feedback: You give up some breadth, but you aim at the users most likely to love you. This is close to what Superhuman did.

options.text: Launch widely anyway. More users will give you clearer data
options.feedback: You get more data fast, but you also spend on users who leave, and a weak first impression is hard to undo.

cards.title: The fans had something in common.
body: Vohra split the answers by the type of user. The "very disappointed" group clustered: founders, executives, managers and business development people. They lived in their inbox all day.
Looking only at users like them, the score rose to about a third without changing the product at all.
Then he asked the fans one more question: what is the main benefit you get? The most common answer was **speed**.

cards.title: Measure fit by what people would miss
body: **Product-market fit** means a group of customers needs your product so much they'd struggle without it.

Growth expert Sean Ellis turned that into one question: how would you feel if you could no longer use this? If around 40% of real users say "very disappointed," fit is likely. The test measures *loss*, not liking. Plenty of people like things they'd never miss.

image.label: Three answer buckets: very, somewhat, not disappointed
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 세 개의 통에 "Very disappointed", "Somewhat disappointed", "Not disappointed" 라벨. 첫 번째 통 옆에 "40%" 기준선 표시. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Split the roadmap in two.
body: Superhuman used the answers to decide what to build.
Half the effort went to doubling down on what fans loved, making the app even faster. The other half went to the "somewhat disappointed" users who also valued speed, fixing what held them back.
Users who didn't care about speed were set aside. The team kept running the survey and tracked the score as a key number.

cards.title: From 22% to 58%.
body: As the team kept building for its best-fit users, the share who'd be very disappointed climbed well past the 40% mark, according to Vohra's own account.

cards.title: A survey is a signal, not proof.
body: The 40% line is a rule of thumb from comparing startups, not a law. Ask only people who have really used the product recently, or you measure curiosity.
Small samples swing wildly. And what people say can differ from what they do, so check the score against whether customers keep coming back.
Finally, a loving segment can be too small to build a business on.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You do monthly bookkeeping for small businesses. You run the same survey. Overall, 25% would be very disappointed to lose you. Among restaurant owners it's 50%. They say the main benefit is tracking food and wage costs every week.
What's your next move?

options.text: Cut prices for everyone to lift satisfaction across the board
options.feedback: You may raise the average a little, but you lose margin and still don't give anyone a reason to love you.

options.text: Build on weekly cost tracking, and fix what stops similar clients from loving it
options.feedback: You narrow your focus but keep existing clients paying while you grow toward the group that needs you most.

options.text: Drop every non-restaurant client this month
options.feedback: The focus is right, but you'd give up income you don't need to lose. You can aim the roadmap without firing anyone.

cards.title: Ask who would miss you, then build for them.
body: Fit isn't a feeling. Ask how disappointed customers would be without you, split the answers by group, and let the fans show you what to improve.
**Try it today:** ask five regular customers how they'd feel if you closed tomorrow. Note who says "very disappointed" and what they have in common.
